title: The Heavy Lifter Who Started Gudumba at Eleven — Cirrhosis, Ascites, and Twenty Kilograms Lost

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is 41 years old, presenting with four months of yellowing of the whites of his eyes. He had been entirely normal four months earlier when he first noticed the yellowing, along with afternoon fatigue that improved with rest. Over the following month he developed abdominal distension, then swelling in his legs, and now facial puffiness. He denies itching or constipation but occasionally passes pitch-black, solid stools. For the last ten days he has had breathlessness, without paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, exercise intolerance, cold hands, palpitations, cough, or wheeze. He has also had frothy urine and occasional blood in his urine, with lemon-yellow urine discoloration, but no painful urination or changes in urine volume.

His work involves heavy weightlifting. He has used alcohol since age 11, starting with a homemade brew called gudumba and, after it was made illegal about a decade later, switching to a branded whiskey — now up to 180 ml daily. He has never smoked and denies other recreational drug use. His bowel and bladder habits are otherwise normal and his diet is mixed, though over the last ten days he has lost his appetite, and he has lost nearly 20 kg involuntarily over the four months. He took herbal medicine for ten days. He has no known hypertension, diabetes, asthma, thyroid disease, or tuberculosis.

**Working diagnosis at presentation:** portal hypertension secondary to cirrhosis of the liver associated with chronic alcohol use disorder, with coronary artery disease leading to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction also considered.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **General exam:** conscious and well-oriented; icterus present; bilateral pitting pedal edema up to the knees (grade 3)
- **Vitals:** temperature 98.3°F, pulse 86 bpm, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min
- **Abdominal exam:** distended abdominal veins visible; soft and distended abdomen with tenderness in the right and left lumbar regions; abdominal girth 94 cm; mild to moderate splenomegaly; hepatomegaly (18 cm span); shifting dullness present
- **Cardiovascular exam:** mildly elevated JVP; a pansystolic, crescendo-decrescendo murmur best heard at the right and left parasternal borders
- **Other findings:** gynecomastia present; upper body segment longer than lower segment (21 cm vs 18 cm)
- **Blood counts:** hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, total leukocyte count 3,400 cells/cumm, platelets 1.20 lakh/cumm
- **Renal function:** blood urea 36 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
He was started on carvedilol, furosemide, lactulose, a multivitamin, and iron supplementation, with plans for upper GI endoscopy. Over the following days, his jaundice and abdominal distension persisted while his pedal edema and facial puffiness subsided and his appetite improved.

Abdominal ultrasound confirmed a nodular liver surface with an enlarged portal vein and loss of its normal flow pattern, consistent with portal hypertension, along with gross splenomegaly and moderate ascites — findings in keeping with chronic liver disease. Ascitic fluid analysis, obtained by tapping 500 mL, showed a high serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG 2.18), consistent with portal hypertension as the cause of his ascites.

His liver function tests showed a markedly elevated bilirubin (total 20.16 mg/dL, direct 14.37 mg/dL) with low albumin (2.3 g/dL). His abdominal distension fluctuated over the following days despite continued diuretic and lactulose therapy, and a further large-volume ascitic tap (1.5 liters) was performed with IV fluid support, while he continued on carvedilol, furosemide, lactulose, and multivitamin and iron supplementation, with upper GI endoscopy still planned to evaluate for varices.
